newsitem.title: FRANCE: US, France to argue "not in front of the children".
newsitem.headline: US, France to argue "not in front of the children".

text.p: Washington and Paris have agreed to discuss differences on NATO reforms and enlargement discreetly -- "not before the children", French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Tuesday.

De Charette acknowledged on RTL radio after U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's visit on Monday that the United States and France had not solved differences on the enlargement of NATO and the sharing out of the alliance's commands.
"We agreed that we should discuss them frankly and try to settle them amicably between us. She said 'not before the children', that was warm and friendly," he said.

Albright left Paris on Tuesday for Brussels to take part in her first meeting of NATO foreign ministers, aiming for reaffirmation of the allies' unified position on enlargement before her talks with Russia later this week.

She said after her 90-minute meeting with French President Jacques Chirac that it had shown "how close the relationship is with our oldest ally", adding: "There are sometimes disagreements between brothers and sisters."

U.S. and French officials have made clear there was no progress in substance either on France's call for Washington to hand over the alliance's southern command, controlling the Mediterranean, to a European, or on Chirac's idea for a five-power summit to overcome Russian hostility to the enlargement of NATO.
De Charette appeared less insistent on the "mini-summit" idea. "We'll see during the process when and how it can be done," he said.
But he proposed that Russia and other ex-communist states take part in a NATO summit in Madrid in July.

"We hope that the Madrid summit will at one point gather Russia and all the countries which do not belong to the alliance and want to join, and even those who do not have plans to join immediately, therefore all European countries," he said.

France and the United States agree the Madrid summit should invite a first wave of former Warsaw Pact countries to become members of the Western alliance. But France wants Romania added to Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia as candidates for that first wave.
De Charette said he was more optimistic than two weeks ago that Paris could achieve its demands for a greater European role in the alliance, but he appeared prepared to put them on the back burner.
"It's not done and if we cannot achieve it, we'll put it off for later. It is not a tragedy but we hope we can achieve it," he said.
Denying there were any differences between Paris and Washington on Zaire, de Charette hinted at a joint initiative soon in the region.

"We are working hand in hand...to try to get central Africa, Zaire and the countries in the region from the difficuties they are facing," he said. "This is a permanent task that you will see in the coming weeks," he added.
Commenting on the current visit to France of Russian General Alexander Lebed, de Charette said he would not be received by government officials but France was aware of his potential role at home.
"Mr Lebed certainly has a role to play in Russia today and tomorrow," he said.

The former Russian security chief is scheduled to meet the speakers of the French National Asembly and Senate and various politicians. On Monday he met the governor of the Bank of France, Jean-Claude Trichet. REUTER
